title: America’s Motherhood Peak: What First Birth Rates Reveal About Future Childlessness
gist: Decomposing US fertility by birth order rather than by age alone, the authors show the 'delayed motherhood' hypothesis has broken: first birth rates are falling at nearly every age, including the early 30s (since 2007) and late 30s (since 2014), with the rate at which childless women become mothers at 30 down 33% since 2015. Holding current first birth rates constant implies lifetime childlessness rising toward 25%, meaning the US is at peak motherhood now rather than merely postponing it.

themes.theme: Why TFR and age-specific rates mislead

insights.claim: The US total fertility rate recently fell to 1.6 births per woman, but broad measures like TFR mask important differences across age groups and birth orders and cannot answer whether more women will end up childless.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: Do not forecast household formation or long-run consumption from TFR alone; birth-order decomposition changes the conclusion.
insights.quote: But broad measures like the total fertility rate can mask important differences across age groups and birth orders.

insights.claim: In 2024 more than 70% of births to US women over age 30 were second or higher-order births, so generic fertility rates for women in their 30s and 40s measure family expansion rather than entry into motherhood.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: The measurement edge in this piece: rising 30s fertility was never evidence of delayed first births, and analysts who used it drew the wrong conclusion.
insights.quote: In 2024, for example, more than 70% of births to women over age 30 were second or higher-order births.
insights.locator: Yet overall fertility rates—even when examined by age

insights.claim: Rising ages at childbirth do not mechanically translate into more childlessness — whether delay becomes foregone motherhood depends on social, economic and institutional conditions.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: The delay-to-childlessness link is conditional, so policy and labour-market conditions are the variables that determine the terminal outcome.
insights.quote: Rising ages at childbirth do not necessarily translate into more women remaining childless.
insights.locator: This "delayed motherhood" hypothesis squares with much historical data

insights.claim: Between 2000 and 2019 the percentage of US women reaching age 45 who had become mothers actually rose from 85% to 91%, meaning delayed childbearing historically coincided with a higher, not lower, share of women becoming mothers.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: The historical base rate that made the delay hypothesis credible — and the benchmark against which the current break should be measured.
insights.quote: Between 2000 and 2019, the percentage of women reaching age 45 who became mothers rose from 85% to 91 percent.
insights.locator: Indeed, until recently in the U.S., the opposite appeared to be true

themes.theme: First birth rates are falling at every age

insights.claim: First birth rates among US women in their early 30s have been declining since 2007, and among women in their late 30s since 2014 — the ages that previously offset declines among women in their teens and 20s.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: The offset mechanism that kept completed motherhood stable has been broken for nearly two decades — this is structural, not a post-pandemic blip.
insights.quote: First birth rates among women in their early 30s have been declining since 2007. For women in their late 30s, first birth rates have been falling since 2014.

insights.claim: Since 2015 the rate at which childless US women became mothers at age 30 has fallen by 33%, while the rate at which childless women became mothers at age 40 has fallen by 13%.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: A 33% decline in the single most important conversion rate for household formation over one decade — the hardest number in the piece.
insights.quote: since 2015, the rate in which childless women became mothers at age 30 has fallen by 33%, while the rate in which childless women became mothers at age 40 has fallen by 13 percent

insights.claim: Entry into motherhood is falling across nearly every age with only negligible increases among women in their mid-to-late 40s — the opposite of what the delayed-motherhood hypothesis predicts.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: Kills the reassuring 'they're just postponing' interpretation that has underpinned benign long-run demographic forecasts.
insights.quote: If women were merely delaying motherhood, we would expect first birth rates among such women to be rising. Instead, entry into motherhood is falling across nearly every age
insights.locator: If women were merely delaying motherhood

insights.claim: First births to US women in their late 40s remain almost non-existent, with fewer than 3 out of every 1,000 childless women becoming mothers in a given year at that age.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: Caps the ceiling for late-life catch-up births — fertility technology is not currently moving this number enough to offset earlier declines.
insights.quote: fewer than 3 out of every 1,000 childless women become mothers in a given year
insights.locator: First births to women in their late 40s remain almost non-existent

themes.theme: Peak motherhood and the 25% childlessness projection

insights.claim: Completed entry into motherhood — the share of women who became mothers by the end of their childbearing years — has already fallen by two percentage points in the past five years among the cohorts now aging out of their reproductive years.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: The turn is already visible in completed cohort data, not just in projections — the trend has moved from forecast to fact.
insights.locator: The first signs are already visible among the women currently aging out

insights.claim: IFS senior fellow Lyman Stone predicts 1-in-4 US women will not become mothers, and the authors' own constant-rate calculation independently produces the same result: lifetime childlessness rising toward 25%.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: A 25% childlessness rate reshapes long-run demand for housing size, education, childcare, elder care and the dependency-ratio path for entitlements.
insights.quote: If current first birth rates persist, lifetime childlessness will rise toward 25 percent.
insights.locator: Lyman Stone, senior fellow at IFS, predicts

insights.claim: The authors call holding current first birth rates constant a conservative estimate because conditional first birth rates are still falling for nearly every age group, so the 25% figure is a floor rather than a central case.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: Risk is skewed to worse-than-25% outcomes; stress-test demographic assumptions above that level rather than below.
insights.quote: Holding rates constant is a conservative estimate.
insights.locator: Holding rates constant is a conservative estimate

insights.claim: The authors state there is no evidence so far that later-age births will make up for current declines, and conclude the United States is likely witnessing peak motherhood today with the share of women becoming mothers falling with each successive cohort.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: Frames a secular, cohort-by-cohort decline rather than a cyclical dip — the assumption to plug into 20-year consumption and labour-force models.
insights.quote: That means we are likely witnessing peak motherhood today.
insights.locator: That means we are likely witnessing peak motherhood today

insights.claim: The authors' estimates are drawn from cumulating cohort age-specific first birth rates, and they note that survey-based estimates of motherhood tend to give lower figures than this method.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: Methodology disclosure matters: their approach is the more optimistic of the two, so survey data would imply an even worse childlessness path.
insights.quote: These estimates are drawn from cumulating cohort age-specific first birth rates. Survey estimates tend to give lower estimates.
insights.locator: 1.  These estimates are drawn from cumulating cohort

themes.theme: Framing and provenance of the argument

insights.claim: The piece reframes falling US fertility from a postponement story into a permanent-foregone-motherhood story, arguing the new first-birth data suggest something far more concerning than delay.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: This reframing is the direction pronatalist policy advocacy will take — expect proposals aimed at first births in the 20s rather than at family size.
insights.quote: New data on first births suggest something far more concerning: more women may never become mothers at all.
insights.locator: For years, falling fertility rates were plausibly interpreted

insights.claim: The analysis is authored by Grant Bailey, Research Fellow and Deputy Director of the Institute for Family Studies' Get Married Initiative, and Anne Morse, who holds a PhD in demography and sociology.
insights.speaker: Grant Bailey and Anne Morse
insights.so_what: Source provenance: this is advocacy-adjacent demography from a marriage-promotion programme, so weight the framing while accepting the vital-statistics inputs.
insights.locator: Grant Bailey is Research Fellow and Deputy Director
